tour.title: Old City: Longshan, Ximending & Dadaocheng
tour.summary: Three centuries of a river town in one wet afternoon — a temple that survived the bombs, a Qing lane that started a feud, a colonial shopping grid, the tea street that paid for everything, the wharf the city forgot, and a night market finale.
tour.overviewText:
Taipei greets you in January with grey sky, wet pavement and a wind off the river that finds every gap in your collar. The city is used to it: the basin was a lake bed, and the drizzle is the price of the green hills that box it in. What the weather hides is age. The towers and the elevated roads are the last fifty years; what you are walking through is the first three hundred.

The city began at its western edge, in a riverside settlement called Bangka. The name is usually explained as an indigenous word for a small boat, which would suit a river port, and nobody has proved it. Bangka sat where the Tamsui River narrowed on its way to the sea, close enough for junks to reach, and by the mid-1800s it was one of the biggest towns in northern Taiwan. The temple you start at, Longshan, has stood there since 1738, built by migrants from Fujian, the Chinese province across the strait, who carried their gods with them the way you might carry your family photographs.

Then the outside world arrived, by force. After the Second Opium War the Qing empire signed the 1858 Treaties of Tientsin and opened Tamsui, the river mouth, to foreign trade; foreign ships began loading in 1862. The cargo that mattered was tea. A British merchant named John Dodd shipped Taiwanese oolong straight to New York in 1869, and within a generation the hills behind the city were terraced with tea bushes and the merchant houses of Dadaocheng were built on the proceeds — which is why the street you will walk has an arcade over the pavement, warehouses behind the shopfronts and baroque faces on 1920s brick.

Japan then ruled this island from 1895 to 1945 and rebuilt the town as a colonial capital: broad straight avenues cut through the old lanes, plus railways, parks and the vast Governor-General's Office that still dominates the avenue. Ximending, the pedestrian district you cross, is a Japanese ward name that outlived its empire — the city gate it is named for was demolished more than a century ago.

The religion you keep meeting is less of a tangle than it looks. Guanyin, the bodhisattva of compassion, holds the main hall at Longshan; Mazu, the sea goddess, shares the building because this was a port; and the City God of Dadaocheng sits in a temple so small it looks like a shop, now the place young Taipei asks for help with love. Politically, the island's official name is the Republic of China; Beijing claims it as a province; most residents favour the status quo. You do not have to settle that question to walk these streets honestly.

The walk is a loose line north: from Longshan and the old lanes of Wanhua, through the shophouses of Dadaocheng and out to the river, finishing at a night market with a bowl in your hand. It is flat, mostly under cover, and best started late morning, so the temples and shops are open and the market is lit by the time you arrive. Every site on it is free; you pay only for what you eat. Carry cash for the stalls, and an EasyCard — Taipei's stored-value transit card — for the metro hops in the middle.
tour.difficulty: Easy. Almost entirely flat, on city pavements and pedestrian lanes. Most of the middle of the walk sits under the covered arcades of Dihua Street, so January drizzle is not a problem. The temples are not step-free — each has a raised threshold and a few steps — and the night market is crowded, uneven and narrow at the busiest hour.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 11am. The temples, Bopiliao and the Dihua Street shops are all open by then, and the walk reaches the river in the last of the afternoon light before finishing at the night market, which only comes alive after half past five. A weekday is calmer than a weekend. If it is raining hard, do it anyway — this is the one route in Taipei built for wet weather.

stops.name: Bangka Longshan Temple
stops.narration:
Bangka Longshan Temple went up in 1738, when the settlers who built it had been in this river town a generation. They came from three counties of Fujian, the province directly across the strait from Taiwan, and they named the temple after the Longshan temple they had left behind at home.

Go in through the Dragon Gate on the right, come out by the Tiger Gate on the left, and do not step on the raised wooden threshold — you are stepping over the spine of the building. The main hall belongs to Guanyin, the bodhisattva of compassion. A bodhisattva is an enlightened figure who has postponed their own release from the cycle of rebirth to help everybody else get out first; in Chinese temples Guanyin is shown as a gentle goddess, which is why she is often taken for one.

The rear hall is the real lesson. Five more deities stand in a row: Mazu, the sea goddess; Guan Yu, the deified general who stands for loyalty; Wenchang, who helps with examinations; Hua Tuo, a physician; and Yue Lao, the matchmaker. Mazu was a real woman, Lin Moniang, born in Fujian around 960, who died young and was said to appear above the water to save sailors. By the Qing dynasty the state had promoted her to Empress of Heaven. A port town worshipped her. That layering — one Buddha, one sea goddess, four specialists — is not confusion. A Taiwanese temple is a phone book of people who handle different problems.

Almost nothing you see is original. Earthquakes and fires wrecked the place repeatedly; today's buildings are a rebuild of 1919 to 1924. On 31 May 1945 American bombers hit the temple and the Guanyin statue was pulled from the burning ruins; locals will tell you she survived with her skirt scorched. Entry is free, and the doors stay open from roughly six in the morning until late evening.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry, as at almost every working temple in Taiwan. Incense, joss money and amulets are sold or offered inside; buy only if you want to take part, and verify current hours at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Usually open daily from about 06:00 to 21:30 or 22:00, with shorter hours around Lunar New Year. Festivals change the schedule — confirm at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level once inside, but every entrance has a raised wooden threshold to step over, and the main hall sits a few steps above the courtyard. Slippery tile floor when it rains.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the back hall before you leave: the row of five specialist deities, including Yue Lao the matchmaker, is the best explanation in Taipei of how folk religion actually works. Then find the small waterfall and pond in the side courtyard, where people rinse their hands.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the Tiger Gate on the left and walk east along Guangzhou Street for about three hundred metres. Where the road bends, a low brick lane opens on your right — that is Bopiliao, the next stop.

stops.name: Bopiliao Historic Block
stops.narration:
This is what Taipei looked like before it was a city: a narrow lane of one- and two-storey brick shophouses, some of them more than two centuries old, and one of the most complete Qing-era streets left in Taipei.

The name is a puzzle. Bopiliao is Pak-phê-liâu in Taiwanese Hokkien, usually translated as skin-peeling hut. One story says animal hides were stripped and tanned here; another says timber had its bark peeled. Nobody has settled it, which is worth knowing, because a great deal of what is told confidently about old Taipei is somebody's best guess.

This lane was the road out of Bangka, the market track toward the interior — and in 1853 it was where Bangka broke. The fighting was called Ding-Xia Jiao, the Top and Bottom cliques, between settlers whose families came from Quanzhou and settlers from Zhangzhou: two neighbouring prefectures in Fujian whose feuds crossed the sea with them. The Quanzhou side lost ground here, moved north, and founded Dadaocheng, the district you are walking to this afternoon. They carried their City God out along this lane. The rest of your walk exists because of a fight that started on this pavement.

The block survived by accident. In 1941 the Japanese colonial government planned an elementary school on this land, and the school grounds walled the old houses off instead of demolishing them. Long after the classrooms emptied, the buildings sat there. Taipei restored the lane between 1999 and 2009, and it reopened as a heritage centre with free exhibitions in the old rooms; the 2010 gangster film Monga, set in Wanhua and named for the district's old Taiwanese name, was shot here and made the place famous.

Entry is free, and the arcade is the best shelter on a wet day. Hours are usually nine to six, Tuesday to Sunday, closed Monday — check the gate, because exhibition rooms close between shows.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free admission to the block and its exhibitions. Verify opening days at the gate: it closes Mondays and between exhibitions.
stops.openingHours: Typically Tuesday to Sunday, about 09:00 to 18:00, closed Monday. Spaces also shut between exhibitions and on public holidays — confirm before counting on it.
stops.accessibility: Level brick lane, no steps along the main stretch. The lane is narrow and the surface is uneven old brick, so take care when wet. Some interiors have a step at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the two odd spaces the Japanese era left behind: a small plaza holding an old fire-fighting reservoir, and a tapering trapezoidal square where a road was cut through. They make sense only once you know the street predates the street plan.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk back out to Guangzhou Street and head north-east for about twenty minutes — roughly a kilometre up Kangding Road and Chengdu Road — to the Ximending pedestrian zone. If the rain has set in, ride instead: one stop from Longshan Temple to Ximen on the blue line, about NT$20.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: lienyuan lee, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ximending Pedestrian Zone
stops.narration:
This district is named after a gate that no longer exists. Under Japanese rule the ward was Seimon-chō, the West Gate district — the area outside the Qing city wall's western gate. Taipei's wall went up in 1884, five kilometres of rammed earth and stone, five gates, and within a decade of the Japanese arriving in 1895 it was being demolished. The West Gate went with them. The Mandarin reading of Seimon-chō survived as Ximending, so the name has outlived the gate by a century.

That demolition is the city you are standing in. The Japanese surveyed Taipei properly, widened the lanes, put in sewers, parks and a railway, and drove broad avenues through the Qing town — the wide roads you have been crossing are colonial engineering. The Governor-General's Office, finished in 1919 and today the Presidential Office Building, is the monument to that programme.

Ximending became Taipei's cinema street in the 1930s. Then the city grew eastward and the district faded, until 1999, when the council banned cars from the lanes and created Taiwan's first and largest pedestrian zone. It worked: three million people shop here in a month; on a weekend the whole area is street-dance crews, buskers and claw machines.

The building that ties it together is the Red House, the low brick octagon ahead. Designed by the Japanese architect Kondō Jūrō, it opened in 1908 as Taiwan's first government-built public market — on what had been an unmarked graveyard, which tells you what the colonial state thought of the site. It now holds a small theatre and a craft market, and these lanes are the heart of Taipei's gay scene and of the city's Pride march.

Nothing here costs anything to wander. Shops run from about eleven in the morning until ten or eleven at night, the food is in the side alleys behind the main drag, and a weekday is calmer than a weekend.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk; you pay only for what you buy. The Red House's shops and small theatre are free to enter, though performances are ticketed. Verify hours at each door.
stops.openingHours: Open street at all hours — the pedestrian zone is closed to vehicles on weekends and holidays. Most shops run about 11:00 to 22:00 or 23:00 daily.
stops.accessibility: Flat, paved and step-free through the pedestrian zone, with dropped kerbs along the main lanes. Crowds, and the parked delivery scooters in the side alleys, are the real obstacle.
stops.insiderTip: The Red House's octagon is easy to walk past because it sits below street level. Go down into the courtyard around it, read the 1908 market history on the ground floor, then eat in the alleys — Taiwanese sausage and rice noodles are the local standards.
stops.nextStopDirections: Ride the MRT rather than walking this one: one stop from Ximen to Beimen on the green line, then about eight minutes on foot north-west to Dihua Street. It is 1.8 kilometres on foot — about twenty-five minutes along busy roads — so the train is the sensible January option.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Multivariable, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Xia Hai City God Temple
stops.narration:
This is a small building doing a large job. A City God — Chenghuang Ye in Mandarin — is not a Buddha and not quite a saint. He began as the guardian of a city's wall and moat, and became the celestial magistrate of its dead, rewarding the honest and punishing the wicked. City gods are chosen from real people who were upright officials in life, because the afterlife is imagined as a bureaucracy and you want competent staff.

This one came from Xia-Cheng, beside the Lin-Hai Gate in Tong'an County, Quanzhou, in Fujian — hence Xia-Hai. In 1821 hundreds of villagers carried the gilded statue across the strait to Bangka. In 1853 the Ding-Xia Jiao fighting you heard about at Bopiliao drove the Tong'an community north, and they brought their god with them, lodging him in a bakery. Thirty-eight men died protecting the statue on that journey; they are worshipped here as the Brave Guards. A general donated the land; the temple went up between 1856 and 1859. One family has looked after it ever since.

The building is about 152 square metres and holds more than six hundred statues — the highest density of deities in Taiwan. You arrive with one specific problem and there is somebody here who handles it. Which explains the crowd at the side altar: that is Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon, the matchmaker who ties an invisible red thread between two people meant for each other. In recent decades this temple became the place Taipei asks about love.

Entry is free and the doors are usually open from about seven to seven. Watch how people pray: three incense sticks, their own name and address spoken aloud, then two crescent moon blocks thrown on the floor for a yes or a no. Ask before you photograph anyone mid-prayer. The tea by the door is free, sweetened by sugar donated by first-time petitioners to Yue Lao.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. This is a working temple, not a ticketed site. Amulets, lamps and offerings cost what they cost, and are never required. Verify hours at the door.
stops.openingHours: Typically open daily, roughly 07:00 to 19:00. It stays busy on the City God's birthday, the thirteenth day of the fifth lunar month, and hours shift around festivals.
stops.accessibility: Tiny, level and crowded, with a raised threshold at the entrance and no room to manoeuvre a wheelchair once inside. Worshippers kneel on the floor in the main aisle.
stops.insiderTip: Watch what people carry out: married couples buy a pair of small fortune shoes for the City God's wife, who is said to keep a husband coming home on time. Single visitors take a red thread from Yue Lao — free, but only after the moon blocks have answered favourably three times.
stops.nextStopDirections: Step back out onto Dihua Street and turn right, walking north along the arcade for about two hundred metres, past the tea shops and the Chinese-medicine shops. Keep your eyes on the shopfronts — the street itself is the exhibit.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: nakashi, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Dihua Street Shophouses
stops.narration:
Look up before you look in: this street is why the old city had a port, and it was built by tea.

First the name. Dadaocheng means the big rice-drying field — Tuā-tiū-tiânn in Taiwanese Hokkien — a village of rice-drying yards on the riverside flats. Dihua Street got its name only in 1947, when the Republic of China government renamed a string of old lanes after places on the mainland; Dihua was the old name of Ürümqi, in Xinjiang. The shops, though, go back to the 1850s, when Quanzhou merchants moved up from Bangka.

What made them rich was a war they had nothing to do with. After the Second Opium War the Qing empire signed the 1858 Treaties of Tientsin and opened Tamsui, the river mouth, to foreign trade; foreign ships began loading in 1862. Tamsui is sixteen kilometres downstream, but Dadaocheng had the deep frontage nearest the city, so the trading houses came here — five British firms by 1872. Then came tea. A British merchant named John Dodd shipped 129,000 kilos of Taiwanese oolong straight to New York in 1869, riding the brand-new Suez Canal. It sold, and within a generation this street was processing the hills behind the city.

Read the architecture as a business plan: each of these is a shophouse — narrow at the street, very deep behind, shop in front, warehouse in the middle, family at the back and above. Over the pavement runs the covered arcade, têng-á-kha in Taiwanese, which keeps goods and customers dry — why this is the best street in Taipei on a wet day.

The facades are a diary: Fujianese brick, Japanese-era baroque pediments, 1960s concrete, glass. The shops sell oolong by weight, ginseng, mushrooms, incense and dried fruit. If your dates run near Lunar New Year — 6 February in 2027 — the street is already stacking New Year goods to the ceiling.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the street. Shops sell by weight — tea and Chinese medicine are usually priced per catty, which is 600 grams — so ask before you commit. Verify opening days on the door.
stops.openingHours: Most shops open about 09:30 to 18:00, some later; a number close on Sundays and many shut over Lunar New Year itself. Hours stretch in the run-up to the New Year market — check the doors as you go.
stops.accessibility: Level under the arcade, which is the point of it, but the pavement is narrow, jammed with stock and customers, and broken in places. Stepping inside a shop usually means one raised threshold.
stops.insiderTip: Buy tea here rather than at a mall, and ask to smell before you do. Then look at the pediment above each door — the date and the family name are often carved into the top, which is the street's own record of who rebuilt after which fire.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west along Minsheng West Road for about two hundred and fifty metres, straight toward the water, until the road ends at the embankment. Go through the Fifth Water Gate in the levee — that is Dadaocheng Wharf, the next stop.

stops.name: Dadaocheng Wharf
stops.narration:
Here is the water that made the city. The Tamsui River is the reason anyone built here at all: Taipei sits in a basin where the Keelung and Xindian rivers meet, and the Tamsui carries that water sixteen kilometres north to the sea at Tamsui. Before railways, and long before the motorway, every sack of tea and every crate of camphor left by boat — and this was the loading point for Dadaocheng.

Then the city turned its back. Through the twentieth century Taipei built embankments along the river and treated it as a drain; for decades the old town's front door was a concrete barrier you could not see over. The change is recent. From 2005 the city began reopening the foreshore, and this wharf is now a promenade, a cycling hub and a stop on the Blue Highway — the river-bus network that still runs boats down to Tamsui when the season and the weather allow. Tickets come from the kiosk on the pier; routes, days and fares change, so read the board rather than a guidebook.

Do not over-romanticise it. This is a working urban river, opaque with silt and tidal, and it still carries the runoff of a city of millions. What it offers is the view and the scale: the Taipei Bridge upstream, the far bank, and in the last hour of light the whole valley going grey and gold.

It costs nothing and never closes, though the weekend food stalls keep their own hours. Cold wind comes straight off the water and there is no shelter at all, so treat this as a ten-minute stop in a January drizzle — then walk east, back into the crowd, and eat.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the wharf. River cruises are ticketed separately and run seasonally, mostly at weekends and in the evening — check the kiosk board for days and fares.
stops.openingHours: The promenade is open at all hours. Weekend stalls, the container market and the river boats keep their own, weather-dependent hours. Verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: A flat, wide, step-free promenade with railings and benches — the most accessible stop on this walk. The wind is the hazard, not the surface.
stops.insiderTip: Turn around once you reach the railing and look back inland: you are looking straight up Minsheng West Road at the waterfront that paid for Dadaocheng. Then walk a minute north along the river path for the clear view of the Taipei Bridge.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back east up Minsheng West Road, then continue along Nanjing West Road for about 850 metres — twelve minutes on foot, past the old round market hall called Jiancheng Circle. The stalls start where Ningxia Road crosses, and that is the final stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Ningxia Night Market
stops.narration:
This is the reason to go out in Taipei after dark. A night market is a street that becomes a kitchen at dusk — a few hundred stalls on gas burners and plastic stools — and by midnight a street again. This one runs along Ningxia Road, named by the post-1945 Republic of China government after Ningxia Province, thousands of kilometres away in northern China.

The market's own history is post-war: there were no food stalls here in the Japanese era; after 1945 people who had lost their jobs set up carts. It sits beside the old Jiancheng Circle, a round market hall built in 1908.

Why here rather than a bigger market? Because Ningxia is small and serious, with one of the highest concentrations of Michelin Bib Gourmand stalls in Taiwan — the guide's award for cheap, excellent food. The award matters less than the queues: a Taipei queue is a local newspaper, and a stall with thirty people in it has earned them.

Now order. Prices are in New Taiwan dollars, and NT$100 buys two or three snacks. Start with an oyster omelette — ô-á-tsian, sweet potato starch with oysters, egg and greens, griddled crisp and cut with a sweet-savoury sauce. Then oyster vermicelli: thin wheat noodles in a thick soup, sharpened with black vinegar. Add a Taiwanese sausage, and finish with braised pork rice, lǔròufàn — pork belly stewed in soy and five spice over rice — the closest thing Taiwan has to a national dish.

Two rules. Bring cash: most stalls do not take cards, and an EasyCard — Taipei's stored-value transit card — is no use at a griddle. And graze — one plate at a time, shared, because the classic mistake is filling up on the first starch you meet. It runs about half past five until midnight daily, though a few stalls take Monday off; read a dark stall as sold out, which is a compliment.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Food is cheap and almost entirely cash: budget around NT$100 per snack, and verify prices on each stall's board before ordering.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 17:30 to midnight, seven nights a week, though individual stalls take days off and many close on Mondays. It is busiest about 19:00 to 21:00 — confirm the day's stalls as you arrive.
stops.accessibility: The road surface is level but the market itself is dense, smoky and narrow, with queues blocking the walking line. Not comfortable by wheelchair at peak hours. There are no seats at most stalls.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the full length once before you buy anything, then commit to the stalls with locals in the queue. Start with the omelette, finish with braised pork rice, and get papaya milk from a drink cart to cool the fried food down.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Eat your way to the far end, then cross to Nanjing West Road for a taxi, or walk five minutes north-west to Shuanglian station on the red line to get home. If you still have appetite in you, the older, rougher Huaxi Street night market is two MRT stops away in Wanhua — but that is a different evening.
